_meta.purpose: Regular-pass MODERNIZATION overlay — the 'every beat gets dressed up' layer. Each entry names a STORY_SCENES sceneKey + act phase and adds cosmetic narration: a speaker nameplate, a tone (drives the speaker-plate accent colour via _actAccentForTone), an optional appended sensory/atmosphere line, and an optional pure-FLAVOR choice (no mechanical effect). Applied at load by _applyStoryFraming AFTER interactions, and it only fills gaps — it never overrides an act that already has an interaction / branches / authored choice. Ships here as data so the modernization pass never edits the 4MB STORY_SCENES literal and stays fully reviewable + revertible.
_meta.shape: { sceneKey, phase, speaker?:'Name', tone?:'cold|villain|dread|grief|mystery|rival|warm|hope|calm|eerie|tender', spriteSide?:'left|right', appendLines?:[..], choice?:{ persistKey, options:[{label,value,reply:[..]}] }, label? }
_meta.tones: warm gold · villain/anger red · dread/eerie/horror violet · mystery lilac · rival/cold blue · grief/sorrow slate · hope green · calm/tender teal

options.label: Memorize the plate. File it for later.
reply: You hold the numbers in your head until they're yours. The lane he means is the one they drew for you — and you've started reading the map they drew it on.

options.label: Say nothing. Just keep walking.
reply: You let it go, for now. Not forgiveness — arithmetic. You haven't earned the right to make it your business yet. Yet.

options.label: Walk beside the cart a little way.
reply: You match its slow pace for a stretch. The Marowak doesn't acknowledge you. But for a few hundred steps the grief has company it didn't ask for and doesn't refuse.

options.label: Let it pass. Keep your own road.
reply: You stand aside and let the cart go by. On this road, grief this common stops getting looked at. You make yourself look until it's out of sight. It's the only thing you have to give.

options.label: Memorize the page of first names.
reply: You read the under-twelve column until it's burned in. He watches you do it, then looks away — he's carried it longer, and it never got lighter with the knowing.

options.label: You've seen enough. Close the ledger.
reply: You shut it. Some pages you don't need twice to never forget. He nods, like he understands the not-looking better than most.

options.label: Set the child's belt back exactly as it was.
reply: You replace it to the millimetre. Let him think the room is still his. You've read it now — that's enough to carry out the door.

options.label: Turn it over, look for the scratched-out name.
reply: You tilt it to the light. The label's been rubbed to nothing by a thumbnail, slowly, over years. A man who keeps nothing kept this — then spent a long time un-naming it. You put it back. Some things aren't yours to know.

inject.speaker: Magma Preacher
appendLines: Heat rises off the dry stump like the ground is breathing through its teeth.

options.label: Pull the Magma flag from the well.
reply: You wrench the staff out of the well's dry throat and lay it flat in the dust. The child watches, expressionless, like they've seen flags come and go.
It changes nothing about the water. It changes one small thing about the silhouette of this place against the sky. You decide that's worth the splinters.

options.label: Leave it. The fight is uphill, not here.
reply: You leave the flag standing. A scrap of cloth doesn't move pipes, and the people who hung it are higher up the route, closer to the heat.
The child keeps pointing at it as you go, as if a thing left standing is a thing agreed to. You don't look back to check whether they're right.

appendLines: The red light moves on his back like something alive is breathing under the mountain.

options.label: Answer him. Tell him how you stop a prayer.
reply: 'You don't stop a prayer,' you tell his back. 'You outlast the one praying it.' He goes very still, as if you've said something he meant to keep for himself.
He doesn't turn. But his lips stop moving, just for a moment, and in the silence the volcano sounds almost ordinary.

options.label: Say nothing. Let the heat hold the silence.
reply: You don't dignify it with an answer. You let his question hang in the rising heat and go unanswered, the way prayers mostly do.
He waits for a reply that doesn't come, and that — the not-coming — seems to unsettle him more than any argument could have.

appendLines: The river slides past low and brown and patient, the way deep water does when it knows it has time.

options.label: Step to the bank. Feel the current for yourself.
reply: You crouch and put a hand in. The pull is gentle and then, an inch deeper, not gentle at all — a steady, indifferent weight that would take you if you let it.
You take your hand back. The grunt watches you do it and grins, like the river already introduced itself and you both heard the same thing.

options.label: Keep your distance from the water.
reply: You stay up on the dry path, where the ground stays ground. The grunt reads the choice and shrugs, unbothered.
'Suit yourself, junior,' he says. 'The current's patient. It doesn't mind waiting for the ones who keep their distance.' The kids laugh. The river says nothing, which is worse.

appendLines: The water comes up over the breach in long, unhurried sheets, the way a thing arrives when it has already won.

options.label: Try to help him close it.
reply: You wade in beside him and put your shoulder to the breach as if a person could shoulder back the sea. The cold climbs to your waist in a heartbeat.
Archie watches you try, and something in his face breaks gently. 'You can't,' he says, almost tender. 'But I'll remember that you got in the water to find out.'

options.label: Stay on dry stone. He opened it; he closes it.
reply: You hold the dry ground at the lip of the breach. The handle was his to hold and the closing is his to do; you won't drown to spare him the weight of it.
He nods, slow, the water rising past his knees. 'Right,' he says. 'Right. No one gets to carry this one but me.' The tide agrees, and keeps coming.

inject.speaker: Galactic Grunt
appendLines: The kiosk hums with a fluorescent calm, the light too even, the way light is in places that never close.

options.label: Ask to see the circled date.
reply: You ask her, flatly, to show you the date. She turns the ledger toward you without hesitation — it's just data; she has no reason to hide it.
You read it. It is, in fact, soon. The duration column says all of it. She watches you do the arithmetic and seems pleased that, at last, someone else is keeping count.

options.label: Don't look. Knowing the date won't move it.
reply: You don't look at the page. A date on a curb won't unhappen for being read, and you'd rather not carry the number up the mountain with you.
She shrugs and logs your refusal — a small notation in the margin, you suspect. To her, even not-knowing is a value she can record.

appendLines: The seam in the sky gives off no light and no dark, only a wrongness the eye keeps trying to correct.

options.label: Tell him the feeling was never the wound.
reply: 'The feeling isn't the wound,' you call up at him. 'It's the proof there was something worth wounding.' He pauses, the way a man pauses over a line of working that won't reduce.
'An interesting error,' he says, finally, and goes back to the seam. But he said error, not nonsense — and an error is a thing that can, in principle, be corrected.

options.label: Don't engage the math. Just climb.
reply: You don't answer the seam or the man addressing it. There is no sentence that reaches him; there is only the distance left between you and the summit.
You close that distance instead. He goes on comforting the universe, unbothered, certain you are a formality. Let him be certain. You keep climbing.

inject.speaker: Plasma Sage
appendLines: The grass is wet enough to soak through a child's shoes; the sage's robes stay dry.

options.label: Read a donor card pinned to the canvas.
reply: The card thanks a benefactor for 'making liberation sustainable.' The phrasing is the part that lingers.
Sustainable. As in: this is built to keep happening.

options.label: Watch the loading dock instead.
reply: You count the crates going out the back against the cheers going up out front. The numbers match exactly.
Matching numbers, you've learned, are the signature of a thing run on purpose.

options.label: Take the last journal page with you.
reply: You fold the page small and put it where you keep things you mean to give back someday.
Someday is doing a lot of work in that sentence. You know it. You take it anyway.

options.label: Leave the journals exactly as you found them.
reply: You square the stack the way it was, key back under the loose board, lock turned soft.
If he ever comes back for them, he should find them waiting, undisturbed, the way nothing else in his childhood ever was.

inject.speaker: Flare Grunt
appendLines: His sunglasses are mirrored; you watch yourself be appraised in them.

options.label: Sit. Finish someone's abandoned meal.
reply: You sit in a stranger's chair and eat a stranger's lunch in a town with no strangers left in it.
It tastes fine. That it tastes fine is somehow the worst report you could file.

options.label: Close the doors as you leave.
reply: You go door to door pulling them shut, the way you'd close the eyes of the sleeping.
It changes nothing. The truck already came. But an open door felt like an invitation to whatever takes next.

options.label: Stay to hear if your name is read aloud.
reply: You wait through a hundred names for your own, and when it comes it sounds like any other syllable in the man's mouth.
That's the horror you take with you: it cost the reader nothing to say it.

options.label: Walk before the reading reaches you.
reply: You turn and go while the list is still in the early districts, before it can reach the page with you on it.
Not hearing it doesn't unprint it. But you decide which voice gets to say your name, and it won't be his.

options.label: Leave a coin tucked behind the poster.
reply: You wedge a coin behind the BIG BAD side, where only someone taking it down would find it.
Not charity. Closer to a vote: somebody saw the good hand, and thought it was worth something.

options.label: Take a photo of the brave side only.
reply: You photograph BIG BAD and nothing else, the way the artist meant it to be seen.
Some bravery you honor by not turning it over, even when you know what's on the back.

options.label: Walk a block beside the one dragging it.
reply: You don't take a corner of it. You just walk the same direction, slow, so they aren't the only thing moving on the street.
They don't acknowledge you. At the corner they go one way and you go the other, and that's the whole of it, and it was something.

options.label: Look away. Give the grief its privacy.
reply: You find something else to look at and let them drag the thing unwatched.
Some weight a person needs to carry without an audience. You give them the empty street and keep going.

appendLines: Somewhere a counter ticks up. It does not care which column you land in.

options.label: Scratch the Impidimp's ears.
reply: It leans into your hand and won't let Marnie's sleeve go.
For one second the Daycare is just a room with a small warm thing in it, and nobody is being sold.

options.label: Let it keep holding onto her.
reply: You don't reach for it. It already chose its person, and its person needs the holding more than you need the proof of being trusted.

options.label: Hold his gaze until he looks away.
reply: He doesn't look away. He just files your face for later, the way he files everything, and keeps smiling.
You learn something about patience from a man who has never once needed it.

options.label: Look at the envelope instead of the man.
reply: You read the weight of it in the older member's hand - a mortgage in an envelope, loyalty by the centimetre.
The man with the lanyard notices what you're noticing. He is still not concerned.

appendLines: The brand color is warm to look at and cold to stand under. Nobody mentions the difference.

options.label: Sign nothing. Pocket the congratulations half.
reply: You tear the packet along the fold and keep only the part that's just words. The blanks with your name in them go in the bin.
The bin is also co-branded. There is no edge of this you can stand outside of.

options.label: Read the offer to the very last page.
reply: You read all of it, slowly, the way the retired trainer told you to. The page near the back is there, of course - the one about how you'll be remembered.
Knowing where the trap is doesn't move it. But you'd rather walk in with your eyes open than out with them closed.

options.label: Stay standing.
reply: You don't sit. He notices, and files it, and offers nothing more - which is its own kind of answer.
Standing costs your legs nothing and costs the moment everything he wanted from it.

options.label: Take the seat. Hear him all the way out.
reply: You sit. He relaxes a degree, mistaking the chair for agreement, and tells you more than he meant to.
Comfort is a tool he reaches for without thinking. You let him hand it to you and you keep your own counsel under it.

options.label: Copy down the small list of teacher names.
reply: You write the small names into your own book, under the others you've started keeping.
The board never meant for anyone to do that. You do it anyway. Someday the lists will be for something.

options.label: Leave the board exactly as it is.
reply: You leave it. The big names stay blamed, the small names stay comfortable, and you carry the shape of it out in your head instead.
Some things you don't need on paper to never forget.

options.label: Read the unfiled resignation letter.
reply: You read it through. It's beautifully written - two years too late, and fluent in the small print that left the kids defenceless.
The craft of it is the worst part. People this good at words chose to spend them on 'personal.'

options.label: Leave it on the desk, unread.
reply: You set it back down where it lay. You don't need the wording to know the shape of what it didn't say.
Two years of 'kids work it out,' then a quiet exit on a personal note. The desk keeps its letter. You keep your contempt.

appendLines: The line they keep mouthing is about coming home safe.

options.label: Look closer at the wet crate.
reply: You crouch and look. You learn nothing you can prove and everything you can't unfeel.
The stain has a smell. You back away from it slower than you'd like to admit.

options.label: Walk on. Don't open it.
reply: You keep walking. Whatever's in the wet crate stays the broker's business, not yours.
The not-knowing rides with you for miles, which is its own kind of weight.

options.label: Measure yourself against the hole.
reply: You stand at the edge and you can't help it — the length is exactly yours.
You step back from the rim before your feet decide anything for you.

options.label: Turn away from the digging.
reply: You make yourself turn before the Marowak's patience becomes contagious.
Behind you the bone-tool sound goes on, unhurried, certain of its appointment.

appendLines: The festival it's meant for ended weeks ago.

options.label: Hold the mask's gaze through the glass.
reply: You hold the look. The glass is cold and the mask is patient and it is in no hurry to win.
You leave first. You always leave first; that, you understand, is the arrangement.

options.label: Step back. Break the staring.
reply: You make yourself step back, the way you'd step back from a ledge.
It lets you, which is somehow worse than being held.

options.label: Leave the money where she'll find it.
reply: You tuck the coins under her tray while she's mid-pull. It won't be enough; nothing is.
You go before she turns, so it can stay a kindness and not a conversation.

options.label: Keep your coins. It changes nothing.
reply: You pocket your own money. A face that fits costs more than a stranger's pity, and you know it.
She doesn't notice you either way. That's the part that follows you out.

appendLines: Someone re-tapes the corners every season so it never quite comes down.

options.label: Call out to the children.
reply: You call. Not one head turns; the row keeps its neat, unblinking pace.
The Hypno, though — the Hypno looks back at you, mild and unbothered, as if noting your name for later.

options.label: Stay silent. Let them pass.
reply: You hold your tongue and let the line walk on into the afternoon.
Saying nothing feels like complicity. Saying something felt like volunteering. Neither feels clean.

options.label: Reach out and touch your own name.
reply: Your fingertip finds the line with your name and next Thursday's date. The ink is dry. The ink is old.
You take your hand back as though the page were warm. It isn't. You wish it were; warm would mean recent.

options.label: Close the ledger. Don't dignify it.
reply: You shut the book on your own date and slide it back across the desk.
The librarian doesn't stop you. Patient lists don't need to be looked at to keep counting.

appendLines: The lace is still tied in a careful double knot.

options.label: Hum the next bar back to them.
reply: You give them the line that comes next. They falter, because they know it's right and don't know how you do.
For a moment the two of you share a song neither of you should have. Then you both stop, fast, like dropping something hot.

options.label: Pretend you don't recognize it.
reply: You let your face go blank and say it's a pretty tune. They believe you, or want to.
The song stays in your teeth all the same, learned now whether you admit it or not.

options.label: Promise the blank stone an ending.
reply: You tell the clearing, quietly, that you'll give the last stone a story that finishes.
The Phantump doesn't react. Promises to the unfinished are heard, you suspect, more than answered.

options.label: Leave the blank stone where it lies.
reply: You leave it blank. It isn't yours to finish, and you're afraid of finishing it wrong.
Walking out, you feel the empty stone behind you the way you feel a held breath.

appendLines: The tape has been pressed and re-pressed so many times the paper has gone soft.

options.label: Straighten the drawing on its tree.
reply: You press all four corners flat again, the way its maker did, so the wind can't have it.
It's a small thing to do for a love that big. You do it anyway.

options.label: Leave it exactly as it was.
reply: You don't touch it. Someone placed it just so, at just that height, for just that pair of eyes.
It isn't yours to fix. You only got to see that it was loved. That was enough; that was the whole gift.

options.label: Set a few of your own coins beside his.
reply: You slide a small stack next to his without a word, the way you'd sit beside someone so they aren't alone.
He doesn't turn. The machine keeps paying. You leave the coins; they're cheaper than the not-knowing what else to do.

options.label: Tell a passing attendant a child is here alone.
reply: You flag someone down and point. The attendant nods, looks, and somehow forgets to walk over.
By the time you glance back, the chair seems to have always been empty. You decide you did the right thing. You decide that twice.

appendLines: The mylar catches the light and throws it back wrong, a little too bright for the grey day.

options.label: Tie the mitten somewhere it can be found.
reply: You knot it high on a fencepost by the path, bright against the grey, where a searching parent's eye might land.
Probably no one comes. You tie it anyway. Hope is cheap and the day already cost too much.

options.label: Take the mitten with you.
reply: You can't make yourself leave a warm thing in cool grass. You tuck it into your pack, against the warm of you.
It stays warm longer than it has any right to. You stop checking after a while. You don't put it down.

options.label: Add a small, kind answer beneath the question.
reply: You print, careful and small: 'Somewhere with no wind, where nobody has to hold on so tight.'
It isn't true. You're not sure it's even kind. But a question that big shouldn't hang at a child's height with nothing under it.

options.label: Leave the question unanswered, like the school did.
reply: You leave it blank under the drawing. Some questions are answered worst by being answered at all.
You walk the hall a little faster. The wobbling letters watch you go, still asking.

appendLines: The red of the cap hums faintly against the tired green of the grass, a color with no business being that awake.

options.label: Add a line of your own beneath the pencil.
reply: You take the pencil and press just as hard: 'and it never gives the body back.'
Two hands now, in the same margin, making the same small stand against the same large thing.

options.label: Leave the page open, the pencil untouched.
reply: You don't add to it. The line is theirs; the margin is theirs; the stand is theirs.
You only weight the guide back against the wind, so the next reader finds the page already open to the truth in pencil.

options.label: Wake the sleeping puppeteer.
reply: You shake his shoulder. He surfaces slow, blinks at the moving puppets, and goes a careful kind of pale.
'They're not supposed to do that on their own,' he whispers. Then the curtain falls and you both, very deliberately, stop talking about it.

options.label: Leave him sleeping. Slip out before the curtain.
reply: You let him sleep. Whatever's running the show is running it better without him, and you don't want to be in the room when it notices you noticed.
You're gone before the applause dies. You don't hear how the show ends. You prefer not to.

appendLines: The fabric is colder than the dirt it came out of, and stays cold in your palm.

options.label: Keep the patch. Carry the cold.
reply: You zip it into the pack. The cold of it travels through the canvas for a while, then settles, like it's gotten comfortable.
You'll forget it's there. It won't forget it's there.

options.label: Bury it deeper. Let the dirt keep it.
reply: You push it back under, deeper than you found it, and tamp the dirt flat with your heel.
A number that low should stay buried. Your hand stays cold the rest of the route anyway.

options.label: Try the case, just once.
reply: You test the catch. Locked, of course, the good kind of locked, the kind chosen on purpose.
You stop trying. Some doors are meant to stay shut from both sides. You let this be one.

options.label: Set the case down and walk on.
reply: You set it back exactly where it lay, the window facing down, the three pages hidden again.
You were meant to read three pages and no more. You honor the count. You don't look for a fourth.
